questions.prompt: Emna is making a word puzzle of her own out of the vocabulary of lesson 12. Her clue reads: "the respect every human being is owed, and that nobody can buy" — seven letters. Which word answers it?
questions.explanation: "dignity" is the word: it names exactly the respect a person is owed simply because they are a person, and the self-respect they keep whatever they earn — and it has the seven letters the clue asks for. "tyranny" also has seven letters, but it names the cruel and unjust use of power over people; it is one of the things that takes dignity away, not the respect itself. "anarchy" names the state of a place where no law is obeyed and nobody is in charge — a question of order, not of respect. And "calamity" means a disaster or a very great misfortune, which is a different idea again, and it has eight letters, so it would not even fit.

questions.prompt: In lesson 13 you sorted a box of words into three columns, one for each of the sounds printed in colour. Which of these four words carries the same vowel sound as the o of "other", /ʌ/?
questions.explanation: "money" is the one: its o is said /ʌ/, the very same short vowel as in "other" and "love". The letter o hides that sound in a whole family of common words — love, money, other, trouble, one. "around", "doubt" and "proud" all carry /aʊ/ instead, the wide sound you make when the mouth opens and then closes on itself. The spelling is the trap here: ou gives /aʊ/ in these three words but /ʌ/ in "trouble" and "young", so the ear, not the eye, has to decide.

questions.prompt: Nizar has two facts to join in a written composition: "The shop had no receipt for the phone." and "The manager refused to change it." He wants to use "therefore". Which line is punctuated the way English requires?

options.text: The shop had no receipt for the phone, therefore the manager refused to change it.
The shop had no receipt for the phone; therefore, the manager refused to change it.
The shop had no receipt for the phone therefore the manager refused to change it.
The shop had no receipt for the phone, therefore, the manager refused to change it.

questions.explanation: "The shop had no receipt for the phone; therefore, the manager refused to change it." is the correct line. "therefore" is an adverb, not a conjunction: it points back at what has just been said but it holds nothing together, so the first clause has to be closed with a semicolon (or a full stop) and the adverb takes a comma after it. "The shop had no receipt for the phone, therefore the manager refused to change it." leaves two complete clauses separated by nothing but a comma, which is the comma splice English forbids. "The shop had no receipt for the phone, therefore, the manager refused to change it." adds the comma after the adverb but keeps the comma in front, so the two clauses are still joined by a comma alone. And "The shop had no receipt for the phone therefore the manager refused to change it." runs them together with no mark at all.

questions.prompt: A teacher has written this rule in the school register: "Students must not eat in the laboratory." She now has to put it on a notice by the door, as an order addressed to the students themselves. Which line does she write?

options.text: You don't eat in the laboratory.
Don't to eat in the laboratory.

questions.explanation: "Don't eat in the laboratory." is the notice: a negative imperative is don't followed by the base verb, with no subject written, because the person addressed is the one standing in front of the notice. "You don't eat in the laboratory." puts the subject back and turns the order into a statement — it now describes a habit instead of forbidding anything. "Not eat in the laboratory." drops don't and leaves the verb with nothing to carry the negative. And "Don't to eat in the laboratory." adds a to that no imperative ever takes: after don't the verb stays bare.

questions.prompt: Rania is checking the list before the class trip and wants the others to confirm. Complete her sentence: "Everybody has paid for the tickets, ___"
questions.explanation: "haven't they?" is the tag: the statement is positive, so the tag is negative; the auxiliary of the statement is have, so have comes back; and "everybody" is picked up by they, even though the verb beside it was the singular has. "hasn't he?" keeps the singular of the verb and chooses a masculine pronoun for a group that may contain anybody. "hasn't everybody?" repeats the subject itself, whereas a tag always ends on a pronoun. And "isn't it?" is the all-purpose ending some learners hang on the end of any sentence at all; English builds its tag from the verb it has just used, so a sentence with has can never be tagged with is.
